Here's what I found on Gumiho, the ICML 2025 paper.

**Overview**
The full title is "Gumiho: A Hybrid Architecture to Prioritize Early Tokens in Speculative Decoding." It was published in the Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2025. The authors are Jinze Li, Yixing Xu, Haiduo Huang, Xuanwu Yin, Dong Li, Edith C.H. Ngai, and Emad Barsoum, and the paper is on arXiv as 2503.10135.

**The problem it targets**
Some speculative decoding methods use a draft model with multiple heads to predict a sequence of future tokens, with each head handling one token. The authors point out that existing methods treat every token in the sequence as equally important, use identical head structures, and rely on a single generation mode, either serial or parallel. They argue that early tokens matter more than later ones, because an early error throws away the entire rest of the sequence.

**How the serial and parallel heads are split**
- They prove theoretically that the first tokens in the draft sequence are more important than later ones.
- **Serial heads:** The early draft heads use a more sophisticated Transformer architecture, run serially, to improve accuracy. One paper summary says the first two tokens are generated with sequential Transformers. A vLLM proposal from the authors adds that these two tokens come from an EAGLE-style transformer head, one after the other.
- **Parallel heads:** Later tokens come from several lightweight MLP heads that run in parallel for efficiency.
- In short, the early heads get the stronger model structure and more running time, which improves overall performance. The code is built on Eagle, with modifications and extensions.

**Results**
- The method raises accepted length further with a Full Tree Attention mechanism and reaches up to 3.65x speedup on Vicuna/LLaMA.
- Average speedup across 6 datasets is 2.97x, compared with Eagle-2's 2.74x (Vicuna-7B). On Vicuna 13B it's 3.23x vs. 3.04x for Eagle-2, a 6.3% gain.
- The parallel MLP heads run about 30-40% faster than Transformer heads, with an acceptable accuracy loss since they only produce later tokens.

**Code and vLLM integration**
The official code is at github.com/AMD-AGI/Gumiho, and the repo says that on July 11, 2025, Gumiho was merged into the vLLM framework. There is also a newer RFC to add Gumiho as a vLLM V1 speculative decoding method, submitted by the paper's original authors. It claims lower per-step drafter latency than EAGLE/EAGLE3 when num_speculative_tokens > 2, with similar end-to-end gains in accepted tokens. These two sources don't quite agree on how far the vLLM integration has gone. The repo describes it as merged, while the newer RFC proposes adding it to the V1 engine, so the exact status may be worth checking.

Here's what I found on P-EAGLE (Parallel-Drafting EAGLE) and how it works in vLLM:

## What it is
P-EAGLE is a new speculative decoding algorithm developed by Amazon that extends EAGLE-3 with parallel drafting. The paper (arXiv 2602.01469) is by Mude Hui, Xin Huang, Jaime Campos Salas, Yue Sun, Nathan Pemberton, Xiang Song, Ashish Khetan and George Karypis. It was first posted on 1 Feb 2026.

## The problem it solves
EAGLE drafts autoregressively, which creates a hidden bottleneck: the more tokens you speculate, the more sequential forward passes the drafter needs. P-EAGLE removes this ceiling by generating all K draft tokens in a single forward pass.

## How it works
- At position 1 (next-token prediction), the input pairs the embedding of the newly generated token with h_context, the same as standard EAGLE.
- For positions 2 through K (multi-token prediction), the token embedding and hidden state don't exist yet. P-EAGLE fills them with two learnable parameters: a shared mask token embedding and a shared hidden state.
- **Training:** Training cost grows quadratically with sequence length times the number of parallel positions, which makes long-context training impractical. To get around this, the authors built a framework that pre-computes attention masks and partitions sequences, so gradients can be accumulated within a single sequence.

## Performance
- **Paper:** 1.10–1.36x speedups over autoregressive EAGLE-3 on GPT-OSS 120B, GPT-OSS 20B, and Qwen3-Coder 30B.
- **vLLM blog:** 1.05×–1.69× speedup over vanilla EAGLE-3 with GPT-OSS 20B on B200 GPUs, across MT-Bench, HumanEval, and SpeedBench.
- **Larger K helps more:** Going from K=3 to K=7, P-EAGLE's acceptance length on HumanEval rises by 0.92 (3.02 to 3.94), while EAGLE-3's rises by only 0.38 (2.65 to 3.03).

## Using it in vLLM
- It's been integrated since vLLM v0.16.0 (PR#32887).
- To turn it on, download or train a parallel-capable drafter head and set "parallel_drafting": true in your vLLM serving config.
- Pre-trained P-EAGLE heads are available on HuggingFace for GPT-OSS 120B, GPT-OSS 20B, and Qwen3-Coder 30B.

Here's what I found on P-EAGLE (Parallel-Drafting EAGLE) and how it works in vLLM:

## What it is
P-EAGLE is a new speculative decoding algorithm developed by Amazon that extends EAGLE-3 with parallel drafting. The paper (arXiv 2602.01469) is by Mude Hui, Xin Huang, Jaime Campos Salas, Yue Sun, Nathan Pemberton, Xiang Song, Ashish Khetan and George Karypis. It was first posted on 1 Feb 2026.

## The problem it solves
EAGLE drafts autoregressively, which creates a hidden bottleneck: the more tokens you speculate, the more sequential forward passes the drafter needs. P-EAGLE removes this ceiling by generating all K draft tokens in a single forward pass.

## How it works
- At position 1 (next-token prediction), the input pairs the embedding of the newly generated token with h_context, the same as standard EAGLE.
- For positions 2 through K (multi-token prediction), the token embedding and hidden state don't exist yet. P-EAGLE fills them with two learnable parameters: a shared mask token embedding and a shared hidden state.
- **Training:** Training cost grows quadratically with sequence length times the number of parallel positions, which makes long-context training impractical. To get around this, the authors built a framework that pre-computes attention masks and partitions sequences, so gradients can be accumulated within a single sequence.

## Performance
- **Paper:** 1.10–1.36x speedups over autoregressive EAGLE-3 on GPT-OSS 120B, GPT-OSS 20B, and Qwen3-Coder 30B.
- **vLLM blog:** 1.05×–1.69× speedup over vanilla EAGLE-3 with GPT-OSS 20B on B200 GPUs, across MT-Bench, HumanEval, and SpeedBench.
- **Larger K helps more:** Going from K=3 to K=7, P-EAGLE's acceptance length on HumanEval rises by 0.92 (3.02 to 3.94), while EAGLE-3's rises by only 0.38 (2.65 to 3.03).

MLSys 2026 accepted several papers on speculative decoding (SD). Here are the main ones I found:

**1. Speculative Decoding: Performance or Illusion? (Oral)**
- Authors: Xiaoxuan Liu, Jiaxiang Yu, Jongseok Park, Ion Stoica, Alvin Cheung
- Presented Thu, May 21, 2026 • 9:00 AM – 9:15 AM PDT
- The authors say it's the first systematic study of SD on a production-grade and widely deployed inference engine (vLLM), covering multiple SD variants ($n$-gram, EAGLE/EAGLE-3, Draft-Model, Multi-Token Prediction) across diverse workloads, model scales, and batch sizes.
- Main finding: verification by the target model dominates the execution, while acceptance length varies markedly across output token positions, requests, and datasets. They also found substantial gaps between observed and theoretical upper bounds.

**2. ReSpec: Towards Optimizing Speculative Decoding in Reinforcement Learning Systems (Oral)**
- Authors: Qiaoling Chen ⋅ Zijun Liu ⋅ Peng Sun ⋅ Shenggui Li ⋅ Guoteng Wang ⋅ Ziming Liu ⋅ Yonggang Wen ⋅ Siyuan Feng ⋅ Tianwei Zhang
- It points to three problems with simply adding SD to RL training: diminishing speedups at large batch sizes, drafter staleness under continual actor updates, and drafter-induced policy degradation.
- Result: On Qwen models (3B–14B), ReSpec achieves up to 4.5x speedup while preserving reward convergence and training stability

**3. Beat the Long Tail: Distribution-Aware Speculative Decoding for RL Training (DAS, Oral)**
- From WukLab (UCSD). DAS integrates two key ideas: an adaptive, nonparametric drafter built from recent rollouts using an incrementally maintained suffix tree, and a length aware speculation policy that allocates more aggressive draft budgets to long trajectories that dominate makespan.
- Experiments on math and code reasoning tasks show that DAS reduces rollout time up to 50% while preserving identical training curves

**4. Accelerating Large-Scale Reasoning Model Inference with Sparse Self-Speculative Decoding**
- The paper proposes using the target model itself as a cheap draft model. But instead of using full attention for the draft version, they use sparse attention with top k token selection from the KV cache.
- An attendee's notes report a high acceptance ratio (~6 tokens) and 2x speedup over vLLM. Even achieves higher throughput than Eagle.

**5. Other related papers in the proceedings**
- SpecDiff-2: Scaling Diffusion Drafter Alignment For Faster Speculative Decoding Jameson Sandler, Jacob Christopher, Tom Hartvigsen, Ferdinando Fioretto
- PRISM: Parametrically Refactor Inference for Speculative Decoding Draft Models Xuliang Wang, Yuetao Chen, Maochan Zhen, Fang Liu, Xinzhou Zheng, Xingwu Liu, Hong Xu, Ming Li

The full proceedings list 135 papers and are at proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026. If you want to look at one of these papers more closely, tell me which.

I couldn't find a complete list of ICML 2026 papers on lossless speculative decoding. The search did turn up several speculative decoding posters on the ICML 2026 site, plus some related work you might confuse with them.

**Speculative decoding papers at ICML 2026**

1. **DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative Decoding.** DFlash is a speculative decoding framework that uses a small block diffusion model to draft tokens in parallel. It is now used in practice: by mid-2026, Meta, Poolside, and NVIDIA had released official DFlash drafters alongside their models.

2. **Trajectory-Level Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models.** This adapts speculative decoding to diffusion language models. It builds draft "denoising trajectories" by exploring a tree and checks them block by block in parallel. On whether it is lossless, the authors formally characterize when this approach is exact and identify trajectory drift as the fundamental cost of increased parallelism. So it is exact only under certain conditions.

3. **CSD: Content-aware Speculative Decoding for Efficient Image Generation.** This one is not strictly lossless. It raises the acceptance rate in low-detail parts of an image to speed up generation. To protect output quality, it adds a distribution alignment filter to keep the output in line with the target model, which significantly improves the generative quality.

**Easy to mix up with ICML 2026**

- **Lossless Speculative Decoding Algorithms for Heterogeneous Vocabularies** (Timor et al.) was presented at **ICML 2025**, not 2026. It offers three new methods that remove the requirement that the draft and target models share a vocabulary. All three keep the target model's output distribution unchanged (lossless) and work with off-the-shelf models without extra training. The reported speedup is up to 2.8 times faster on tasks like summarization, coding, and long-document understanding.
- **Other 2026 papers with no confirmed venue.** The Awesome-Speculative-Decoding reading list includes 2026 preprints such as "Overcoming Joint Intractability with Lossless Hierarchical Speculative Decoding" [2026-01], "Learning to Draft: Adaptive Speculative Decoding with Reinforcement Learning" [2026-03], "Speculative Speculative Decoding" [2026-03], and "Cactus: Accelerating Auto-Regressive Decoding with Constrained Acceptance Speculative Sampling" [2026-04]. These results don't say whether any were accepted to ICML 2026. The list's latest conference section is ICLR 2026, so it may not cover ICML 2026 yet.

**Related: does "lossless" hold in practice?**
A NeurIPS 2026 Education Track tutorial questions how well "lossless" has actually been tested. It says that the standard benchmarks cover only a small slice of real-world tasks, and outside them there is no empirical evidence of losslessness. Using OpenRouter traffic data, it finds the tested domains make up only 17% of token usage; the other 83% has never been measured. The tutorial introduces "Losslessbench" to test this.

For a full list, you could search the ICML 2026 virtual site (icml.cc/virtual/2026) for "speculative".

Here's what I found on SpecDiff (Christopher et al., NAACL 2025).

**Paper details**
- **Title and venue:** "Speculative Diffusion Decoding: Accelerating Language Generation through Diffusion," published in the Proceedings of the 2025 NAACL Conference (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 12042–12059, Albuquerque, New Mexico.
- **Authors:** Jacob K Christopher, Brian R. Bartoldson, Tal Ben-Nun, Michael Cardei, Bhavya Kailkhura, and Ferdinando Fioretto.
- **DOI:** 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.601. There is also an arXiv version (2408.05636); the first version came out on 10 Aug 2024 and the fourth on 10 Feb 2025.

**The problem it tackles**
Speculative decoding speeds up generation by checking draft tokens in parallel, but its efficiency remains inherently limited by the reliance on incremental token generation in existing draft models. The paper's fix is a version of speculative decoding that uses discrete diffusion models to write the drafts, so both drafting and verification run in parallel.

**How the diffusion drafter works**
- The drafter is a discrete diffusion model, specifically the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM).
- With a normal drafter, a 32-token draft takes 32 passes, one after another. SpecDiff instead uses a diffusion model that produces the whole block of tokens at once through global denoising.
- Drafting cost depends on the number of diffusion steps (T), not on the draft length (γ). T can be as low as 1 or 2 steps, so drafts can grow to 32 tokens or more without a linear slowdown.
- The output is unchanged: SpecDiff uses the standard draft-then-verify workflow and verification math, so the final text matches what the target model would have produced on its own.

**Experiments and results**
- **Benchmarks:** CNN/DM (summarization), OpenWebText (general language modeling) and MT Bench (instruction following and multi-turn conversation). Target models were GPT-2 XL (1.5B), GPT-NEO (2.7B) and Vicuna (33B).
- **Speedups:** up to 7.2x over standard generation and up to 1.75x over existing speculative decoding approaches.
- **Acceptance rates:** on OpenWebText, SpecDiff kept token acceptance high even with drafts of 20 tokens, where standard methods usually struggle.
- **Compute:** it reportedly uses 33% fewer FLOPs per draft than state-of-the-art autoregressive drafters. This comes from a third-party summary site, not the paper itself.

**Follow-up: SpecDiff-2**
A later paper by Sandler, Christopher, Hartvigsen and Fioretto (arXiv 2511.00606, Nov 2025) builds on this work. It uses discrete diffusion as a non-autoregressive drafter and adds new techniques to calibrate diffusion drafters against autoregressive verifiers. Specifically, "streak-distillation" trains the drafter to produce long runs of accepted tokens, and "self-selection" picks the draft expected to give the highest throughput at test time. That paper describes the original SpecDiff as the previous state-of-the-art speculative diffusion method.

**Links**
- ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.601/
- arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05636
- Project page (covers SpecDiff and SpecDiff-2): https://specdiff.github.io/

The paper you're looking for is **arXiv:2607.05147**, "DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation" (July 2026).

**The problem it addresses**
- Recent parallel drafters can propose long token sequences in one forward pass, but their acceptance rates drop quickly because the tokens don't depend on each other. Verifying all of these long blocks also uses up batch capacity on tokens that are likely to be rejected, which badly hurts throughput when many requests are served at once.
- In DFlash, each parallel position averages over all possible earlier tokens instead of conditioning on the actual sampled prefix. So the model often proposes suffixes that don't fit together, a failure called multi-modal collision (Gu et al., 2018; Stern et al., 2018).

**Sequential correction (semi-autoregressive drafter)**
- The parallel backbone is based on DFlash, which takes key-value features from the target model's layers and injects them into the draft model's hidden space. DSpark then adds a lightweight sequential block to capture dependencies between neighboring tokens without much extra compute.
- In short, the first prediction benefits from a deep parallel model, and later predictions can see what was actually sampled. The default Markov head uses a low-rank transition matrix with rank r=256. An RNN head was also tested, but it added complexity for only small extra gains.

**Confidence estimator and scheduler**
- A confidence head estimates each draft token's chance of surviving target verification, assuming all earlier tokens survived. Multiplying these estimates gives the probability that a whole prefix survives. DSpark then calibrates these cumulative estimates with sequential temperature scaling on held-out data.
- The scheduler greedily admits the prefix extensions most likely to survive, checks a hardware throughput curve after each one, and keeps the setting with the best expected throughput. When load is light, extra checks are cheap; when load is heavy, low-survival suffixes take up scarce batch capacity.

**Results**
- On offline benchmarks, DSpark accepts more tokens per round than Eagle3 and DFlash. In live DeepSeek-V4 serving, it speeds up per-user generation by 60%-85% on V4-Flash and 57%-78% on V4-Pro at matched throughput levels.
- On Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DSpark's accepted length is 27–31% higher than Eagle3 and 16–18% higher than DFlash, and a 2-layer DSpark already beats the 5-layer DFlash.
- At batch size 128, increasing the draft length from 4 to 16 adds only 0.2%–1.3% to full-round latency over DFlash, while accepted length improves by up to 30%.

**Caveats**
- One review notes that the DFlash vs. DSpark comparison doesn't isolate the sequential head, because DSpark also changes the generation design, including how the anchor token is used.
- The authors acknowledge that every request still pays the fixed cost of generating the first block, even complex queries that will accept few tokens. They propose difficulty-aware early exit as the next step.

**Resources:** The paper releases DSpark checkpoints for preview DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Pro, along with the DeepSpec training repository, which contains Eagle3, DFlash, and DSpark. DFlash itself is arXiv:2602.06036 (Chen, Liang, Liu).

The paper you're looking for is **"Mirror Speculative Decoding: Breaking the Serial Barrier in LLM Inference"** from Apple, published as arXiv 2510.13161.

**Authors:** Nikhil Bhendawade, Kumari Nishu, Arnav Kundu, Chris Bartels, Minsik Cho, Irina Belousova (Apple)

**The problem it tackles:** Speculative decoding uses a draft model to look ahead, but its gains are capped by the cost of generating draft tokens one at a time. Bigger drafts get more tokens accepted, but they also add latency, which makes the speed-accuracy tradeoff worse. Earlier methods (Medusa, Hydra, EAGLE) cut some of the draft cost, but they either lower acceptance or add overheads that limit scaling.

**How it works:**
- Mirror-SD launches branch-complete rollouts from early-exit signals in parallel with the target model's suffix, and explicitly maps computation across GPUs and NPUs to exploit cross-device parallelism.
- The draft speculates forward continuations for the target to verify, while the target simultaneously speculates correction paths for the draft. This turns speculation into two complementary execution pipelines.
- The draft model runs on the NPU, which is efficient for approximate inference, while the target model runs on the GPU, which is better suited to high-fidelity, throughput-critical computation.
- It also uses Speculative Streaming (SS), which lets the draft emit multiple tokens per step without changing acceptance semantics.
- The method is lossless: it guarantees the same outputs as the target model under the same decoding process.

**Setup and results:**
- Target models are split across eight M2 Ultra GPUs using Megatron-style tensor parallelism, while the draft runs on eight NPUs.
- On SpecBench with server-scale models (Qwen3-14B/32B, Mistral-24B, OPT-66B), Mirror-SD achieved 2.8× to 5.8× wall-time speedups over target-only autoregressive decoding. That's about a 30% average relative improvement over the strongest baseline, EAGLE3.
- On Qwen3-14B with greedy sampling, it averaged 3.8× acceleration, compared with 2.97× for the strongest prior methods.

**Links:**
- arXiv abstract: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13161 (HTML v2: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13161v2)
- Apple ML Research: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mirror

Here's what I found on the paper **"Overcoming Joint Intractability with Lossless Hierarchical Speculative Decoding"**:

## Publication details
- **Authors:** Zhou, Yuxuan and Huang, Fei and Li, Heng and Wu, Fengyi and Wang, Tianyu and Zhang, Jianwei and Lin, Junyang and Cheng, Zhi-Qi
- **Venue:** International Conference on Learning Representations, 2026 (ICLR 2026)
- **arXiv:** 2601.05724, v1 posted Fri, 9 Jan 2026
- **Code:** https://github.com/ZhouYuxuanYX/Hierarchical-Speculative-Decoding

## The problem
In speculative decoding, verification is a key bottleneck in improving inference speed while maintaining distribution fidelity. Recent work has shown that sequence-level verification leads to a higher number of accepted tokens compared to token-wise verification. However, existing solutions often rely on surrogate approximations or are constrained by partial information, struggling with joint intractability. "Joint intractability" means that simply applying the resampling strategy used in tokenwise verification (Leviathan et al., 2023) would require full joint probabilities over all possible decoding paths to correctly recover the target distribution, which is computationally infeasible.

## The method (HSD)
The authors propose Hierarchical Speculative Decoding (HSD), a provably lossless verification method that significantly boosts the expected number of accepted tokens and overcomes joint intractability by balancing excess and deficient probability mass across accessible branches. It works through hierarchical branch resampling, where multiple resampling distributions at different levels recover partial target distributions, which together statistically recover the full distribution.

The key insight: although joint probabilities of the full space are unavailable, given a prefix, the probabilities for all next tokens in the vocabulary are accessible. In addition, "capping" is used to compress multi-step resampling into a single step.

## Results
- Integrating HSD into EAGLE-3 yields over a 12% performance gain, establishing state-of-the-art decoding efficiency without compromising distribution fidelity.
- HSD consistently outperforms both Tokenwise and Blockwise verification across diverse datasets (GSM8K, HumanEval, CNN/DailyMail) and model scales (14B, 32B, 72B). On HumanEval with a 32B target model, HSD achieves a 12.3% improvement in Block Efficiency and an 11.4% increase in Decoding Speed.
- Overhead is small: verification accounts for less than 1% of total decoding time, with the majority still spent on draft and target forward passes.
- Unlike Blockwise Verification, the method is designed to easily combine with other approaches, such as the widely adopted multi-draft setups.

## Limitations
Like every speculative decoding method, its performance is tethered to the quality of the draft model. Also, the current implementation uses a fixed draft length.

I found the paper: **"Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right"** (arXiv:2510.22876).

**Basics**
- Published October 26, 2025. The authors are Ranran Haoran Zhang, Soumik Dey, Ashirbad Mishra, Hansi Wu, Binbin Li and Rui Zhang. The newest version on arXiv is v3 (arxiv.org/html/2510.22876v3).
- The code is at https://github.com/eBay/spec_dec.

**The ragged tensor problem**
Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by having a small draft model propose several tokens, which a larger target model then checks in parallel. Doing this in batches matters for production serving, but it creates the ragged tensor problem. Sequences in the same batch accept different numbers of draft tokens, which breaks right-alignment and corrupts position IDs, attention masks and KV-cache state. The resulting variable-length tensors don't fit the rectangular operations GPUs handle well.

**Problems with earlier implementations**
- The authors say the widely used HuggingFace implementation produces the same output as standard generation, but only at batch size 1.
- When they tested public batch implementations, BSP (Su et al., 2023) and DSD (Yan et al., 2025) produced repetitive tokens or <unk> symbols under greedy decoding instead of matching standard generation.
- They also say DSD and recent Meta work (Tang et al., 2025) wrongly sample bonus tokens from the draft model's distribution instead of the target model's, which breaks the core correctness guarantee of speculative decoding.

**What the paper contributes**
1. It formally defines the synchronization rules a correct implementation must keep, proves its update rule preserves them, and presents EqSpec, which it calls the first algorithm guaranteed to match the target model's output distribution, because it enforces those rules after every verification round.
2. It shows that the cost of realigning sequences grows faster than linearly with batch size. In experiments, realignment takes up to 40% of computation at batch size 8.
3. It introduces EXSPEC, which keeps a sliding pool of sequences and groups same-length ones together, cutting realignment overhead while keeping each sequence's speculative speedup.

**Results**
On SpecBench, using Vicuna-7B/68M, Qwen3-8B/0.6B and GLM-4-9B/0.6B target/draft pairs, the method reaches up to 3× the throughput at batch size 8 compared with batch size 1, while keeping 95% output equivalence. One review says the remaining mismatches come from floating-point non-determinism and tie-breaking in argmax sampling, not from flaws in the algorithm. The method needs no custom kernels and fits into existing inference stacks.

Here's what I found on the SpecExec paper (arXiv 2406.02532).

**The paper**
- **Title and authors:** "SpecExec: Massively Parallel Speculative Decoding for Interactive LLM Inference on Consumer Devices," by Ruslan Svirschevski, Avner May, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen, Zhihao Jia, Max Ryabinin. The authors are affiliated with Carnegie Mellon University, Meta AI, Together AI, Yandex and HSE University.
- **Dates:** First submitted 4 Jun 2024 (v1); last revised 30 Nov 2024 (v3).
- **Venue:** The PDF confirms it appeared at the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).
- **Code:** github.com/yandex-research/specexec.

**The problem**
Most earlier speculative decoding work implicitly designs its algorithms for high-end datacenter hardware. This paper asks the opposite question: how fast can LLMs run on consumer machines? Consumer GPUs can't fit the largest models (50B+ parameters), so the models have to be offloaded to RAM or SSD. With offloaded parameters, the engine can process hundreds or thousands of tokens in the same time as one token, which makes speculative decoding a natural fit.

**How it works**
- SpecExec is a simple parallel decoding method that can generate up to 20 tokens per target model iteration for popular LLM families. It relies on two things: token probabilities in modern LLMs are very "spiky," and the draft and target models' output probabilities closely agree.
- A powerful draft model deterministically builds a large tree of the most likely continuations, using a parallel search algorithm. The target model treats this tree as a "cache" and validates it in a single pass.
- **Main difference from standard speculative decoding:** the draft tree doesn't need to follow a known probability distribution. SpecExec still produces correct samples with any draft tree, even a deterministic one.
- **The name:** it comes from CPU speculative execution. Modern CPUs predict which operations to compute ahead of time so they use compute cycles better.

**Results**
- With large enough budgets, the draft trees yield 10–20 accepted tokens.
- The system runs Llama 2-70B or similar models interactively on consumer GPUs with offloading: 4–6 tokens/second with 4-bit quantization or 2–3 tokens/second with 16-bit weights. That's a 10–18x speedup over sequential inference on the same hardware.
- **Baseline:** SpecInfer is the main comparison throughout the paper.
- **Engineering tricks:** offloading is sped up by loading the next layer's parameters while the previous layer's activations are computed, on a dedicated CUDA stream. The authors also preload the target model's first few layers onto the GPU in the background while drafting.

**The paper**
- **Title and authors:** "SpecExec: Massively Parallel Speculative Decoding for Interactive LLM Inference on Consumer Devices," by Ruslan Svirschevski, Avner May, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen, Zhihao Jia, Max Ryabinin. The authors are affiliated with Carnegie Mellon University, Meta AI, Together AI, Yandex and HSE University.
- **Dates:** First submitted 4 Jun 2024 (v1); last revised 30 Nov 2024 (v3).
- **Venue:** The PDF confirms it appeared at the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).
- **Code:** github.com/yandex-research/specexec.

**The problem**
Most earlier speculative decoding work implicitly designs its algorithms for high-end datacenter hardware. This paper asks the opposite question: how fast can LLMs run on consumer machines? Consumer GPUs can't fit the largest models (50B+ parameters), so the models have to be offloaded to RAM or SSD. With offloaded parameters, the engine can process hundreds or thousands of tokens in the same time as one token, which makes speculative decoding a natural fit.

**How it works**
- SpecExec is a simple parallel decoding method that can generate up to 20 tokens per target model iteration for popular LLM families. It relies on two things: token probabilities in modern LLMs are very "spiky," and the draft and target models' output probabilities closely agree.
- A powerful draft model deterministically builds a large tree of the most likely continuations, using a parallel search algorithm. The target model treats this tree as a "cache" and validates it in a single pass.
- **Main difference from standard speculative decoding:** the draft tree doesn't need to follow a known probability distribution. SpecExec still produces correct samples with any draft tree, even a deterministic one.
- **The name:** it comes from CPU speculative execution. Modern CPUs predict which operations to compute ahead of time so they use compute cycles better.

**Results**
- With large enough budgets, the draft trees yield 10–20 accepted tokens.
- The system runs Llama 2-70B or similar models interactively on consumer GPUs with offloading: 4–6 tokens/second with 4-bit quantization or 2–3 tokens/second with 16-bit weights. That's a 10–18x speedup over sequential inference on the same hardware.
- **Baseline:** SpecInfer is the main comparison throughout the paper.
- **Engineering tricks:** offloading is sped up by loading the next layer's parameters while the previous layer's activations are computed, on a dedicated CUDA stream. The authors also preload the target model's first few layers onto the GPU in the background while drafting.

**Paper details**
- **Title:** Falcon: Faster and Parallel Inference of Large Language Models through Enhanced Semi-Autoregressive Drafting and Custom-Designed Decoding Tree
- **Authors:** Xiangxiang Gao, Weisheng Xie, Yiwei Xiang, Feng Ji
- **arXiv:** 2412.12639 (cs.CL). It was submitted on 17 Dec 2024; the latest version (v3) is dated 22 Apr 2025.

**The problem it tackles**
Speculative decoding has to trade off two things: keeping drafting latency low and keeping speculation accuracy high. Existing methods draft in one of two ways. Autoregressive (AR) drafting generates tokens one at a time, each depending on the ones before it, which limits parallelism. Semi-autoregressive (SAR) drafting generates several tokens at once, making drafting more parallel. The downside is that SAR drafting can't fully capture how tokens in the same block depend on each other, which can lower the acceptance rate.

**Main contributions**
1. **Coupled Sequential Glancing Distillation (CSGD):** strengthens the dependencies between tokens in the same block, which raises speculation accuracy. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of why this works.
2. **Custom-Designed Decoding Tree:** lets the drafter produce multiple tokens in one forward pass, and run more forward passes when needed. This increases the number of drafted tokens and substantially improves the overall acceptance rate.
3. **Architecture:** According to a survey that discusses the paper, Falcon's drafter takes token embeddings and Transformer features from the target LLM as input, and uses LSTM layers, relaxed causal-masked self-attention, and MLP networks.

**Results**
- The paper evaluates Falcon on MT-Bench, HumanEval, and GSM8K.
- It reports a lossless speedup of 2.91x to 3.51x on the Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat model series.
- The authors say this beats existing speculative decoding methods, including Eagle, Medusa, Lookahead, SPS, and PLD, while the drafter is only about the size of two Transformer layers.

**An outside critique**
Pith, an automated review site, called it a "useful SAR speculative decoding result with a real training contribution, but the headline speedups may be in-sample because the tree and k are tuned on the same benchmarks."

**About AAAI 2025:** None of the pages I found confirm that the paper was accepted at AAAI 2025. They list it only as an arXiv preprint. The paper's format and v3 revision date fit an AAAI 2025 publication, but you should check the AAAI proceedings to confirm the venue.

Here's what I found on **MoESD: Unveil Speculative Decoding's Potential for Accelerating Sparse MoE**.

**Paper details**
- **arXiv ID:** 2505.19645. v1 was posted May 26, 2025, v2 on June 13, 2025, v3 on October 6, 2025, and v4 on February 16, 2026.
- **Authors:** Zongle Huang, Lei Zhu, Zongyuan Zhan, Ting Hu, Weikai Mao, Xianzhi Yu, Yongpan Liu, and Tianyu Zhang, at the 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
- **Venue:** A paper-notes site lists it as a NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight, and there is a NeurIPS poster page for it as well.

**Main argument**
- Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up LLM inference without losing accuracy, but it has been considered efficient only for dense models. The NeurIPS slides use EAGLE paper numbers as the reason: about 1.5x speedup for Mixtral 8x7B Instruct-v0.1 (MoE) versus about 3x for Llama/Vicuna (dense models).
- The authors show that at medium batch sizes, MoE models surprisingly benefit more from SD than dense models. And as MoE models get sparser, which is where MoE design is heading, SD stays effective across a wider range of batch sizes.

**Why it works**
- When the batch size is moderate, all experts are already activated in a single decoding step, so verifying multiple draft tokens doesn't add any extra cost for loading expert parameters.
- In sparser MoEs, each expert processes fewer tokens each time its parameters are loaded, so the GPU's compute units sit underused. That leaves more room for SD to speed things up.

**Contributions**
- A reliable model of SD's tradeoffs, built on theoretical analysis.
- A new metric called "target efficiency," which captures how workload and model architecture affect SD's speedup. It helps researchers find system bottlenecks. Most SD research focuses on acceptance rates, but changes in workload and model architecture can still slow SD down even when acceptance rates are high.
- MoESD doesn't propose a new SD algorithm. It re-examines how SD behaves on MoE models through theory and performance modeling. It uses the most basic chain-style speculation pattern.

**Results and use cases**
- Experiments on several GPUs show up to 2.29x speedup for Qwen2-57B-A14B at medium batch sizes and confirm the theoretical predictions.
- The method suits private serving in particular, where batches typically hold tens of requests. SD can also help when an MoE model is too large to fit in GPU memory.

**Later work**
A 2026 paper, EVICT, builds on this result. It notes that tree-based speculative decoding loses its advantage on sparse MoE models: as the draft tree grows, different branches activate different experts, which makes verification much more expensive.

**Links:** arXiv abstract (arxiv.org/abs/2505.19645), NeurIPS poster (neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119061), and NeurIPS slides (neurips.cc/media/neurips-2025/Slides/119061.pdf).

The sparse self-speculative decoding paper is in the MLSys 2026 proceedings. SwiftSpec is not an MLSys paper; it appeared at ASPLOS '26.

**The sparse self-speculative decoding paper (MLSys 2026)**
- **Where it's listed:** The MLSys 2026 proceedings (Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 8) include "Accelerating Large-Scale Reasoning Model Inference with Sparse Self-Speculative Decoding" by Yilong Zhao, Jiaming Tang, Kan Zhu, Zihao Ye, Chi-Chih Chang, Chaofan Lin, Jongseok Park, Guangxuan Xiao, Mohamed S. I found several surveys and related papers on speculative decoding. Some are from 2026, and others are earlier surveys that set up the main taxonomies.

## 2026 papers

**1. "Is Multimodal Speculative Decoding Ready for Diffusion-Based Parallel Drafting? A Survey and Empirical Diagnosis" (arXiv 2608.20743, Aug 2026)**
- Its starting point is that speculative decoding's lossless guarantee has motivated a line of work that pushes the drafter itself toward parallel generation.
- It points to block-parallel generative drafting, including diffusion-based methods such as DFlash and DSpark, achieving up to 3.6x speedup on common daily chatting tasks.
- **Taxonomy:** a unified taxonomy that isolates drafter-side parallelism from orthogonal design choices such as tree construction and verification strategies. It covers Vision-Language, Video-Language, Audio, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures.
- It also compares methods on benchmarks including OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning.

**2. "A Practical Investigation of Training-free Relaxed Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2607.08690, Jul 2026)**
- This one is about the lossless vs. relaxed trade-off. Standard speculative decoding is lossless: its rejection and resampling steps exactly preserve the LLM's sampling distribution. Recent work argues that relaxing this strict guarantee can yield further speed-ups, controlled capability-speed trade-offs, or even capability gains.
- It includes a taxonomy table of relaxed speculative decoding methods. Main takeaways: relaxation can require considerable capability evaluation unlike lossless speculative decoding, and many relaxed approaches rely on a drafter that is a good language model, making them unsuited for lightweight dedicated multi-token-prediction drafters.
- It notes that multi-token-prediction (MTP) modules are being used more in practice. They frequently appear in LLM releases such as DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron, and GLM.

**3. "Speculative Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2603.03251, Kumar, Dao, May)**
- This is a method paper, not a survey, but it's relevant to the "lossless" part of your query: Like ordinary speculative decoding, SSD is lossless. Unlike ordinary speculative decoding, in SSD the draft model is located on distinct hardware from the target.

**4. Other 2026 surveys**
- "Speculative Decoding for Multimodal Models: A Survey" on Preprints.org (manuscript 202603.2344). The search returned no abstract text for it.
- A technical blog survey (May 2026) that describes speculative decoding as achieving lossless speedup without modifying the target model's output distribution.

## Earlier surveys (still widely cited)

**5. "Speculative Decoding and Beyond: An In-Depth Survey of Techniques" (arXiv 2502.19732, Hu et al., latest v4)**
- It categorize[s] methods based on their generation strategies (from simple n-gram prediction to sophisticated draft models) and refinement mechanisms (including single-pass verification and iterative approaches).
- Its taxonomy decomposes these frameworks into two fundamental phases: Sequence Generation and Sequence Refinement.

**6. "Unlocking Efficiency in LLM Inference: A Comprehensive Survey of Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2401.07851, Xia et al.)**
- It separates lossless from approximate verification. Compared with the lossless criterion, approximate methods slightly relax the matching requirement to trust the drafts more, leading to higher acceptance of drafted tokens.

The paper you're looking for is **"Cassandra: Enabling Reasoning LLMs at Edge via Self-Speculative Decoding"** (arXiv:2605.26558).

**Paper details**
- **Authors:** Soongyu Choi, Yuntae Kim, Muyoung Son and Joo-Young Kim. It was submitted 2026-05-26 under cs.AR (hardware architecture). The paper is also listed on the website of KAIST's CastLab.
- **Links:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26558 (abstract) and https://arxiv.org/html/2605.26558v1 (HTML version)

**The problem it tackles**
The authors argue that as reasoning LLMs increasingly suffer from decode-stage overhead and approximation-based methods degrade accuracy, lossless speculative decoding has become essential for efficient inference. However, existing methods still struggle to deliver strong low-batch performance without additional training, limiting practical deployment on consumer devices.

**How it works**
- **Draft model built from the target model:** The main idea is that a compact yet high-quality draft model can be derived directly from the target LLM through fine-grained data selection, without additional training. Using optimized pruning and mantissa truncation, it identifies the most salient values in both model weights and the Key-Value (KV) cache, enabling rapid candidate token generation before full-precision parallel verification.
- **Exponent compression:** The authors found that the size of the exponent bits limits speed. As two distinct solutions, we propose lossy exponent compression based on the MX format and lossless exponent compression based on unary coding.
- **Hardware support:** To further reduce the overhead of format conversion between Cassandra representations and standard floating-point formats, we also introduce a lightweight encoder-decoder hardware module designed for seamless integration with commercial GPUs and NPUs.
- **No extra training or second model:** Cassandra adopts a training-free self-speculative decoding framework, eliminating the need for additional training while avoiding duplication of model parameters.

**Results**
- Cassandra achieves up to 2.41x speedup over the BF16 baseline without additional training.
- On Llama 3 8B running on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, Cassandra generates 1.81x more tokens under the same memory budget compared to Eagle-3, a state-of-the-art speculative decoding method.
- The authors say it is the first self-speculative decoding framework that leverages algorithm–hardware co-design specifically for low-batch LLM inference on consumer-grade edge devices.

**A caveat from an outside review**
Pith, an automated paper-review site, noted that the supplied text gives no acceptance rates or accuracy numbers to back the lossless claim. That matters because speed gains from speculative decoding depend on how often the draft tokens are accepted. The reviewer only had the abstract, though, and said the full manuscript may contain these numbers.

**Related work**
- **CAS-Spec**, another self-speculative decoding method, was flagged as a very similar paper (CAS-Spec: Cascade Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for On-the-Fly Lossless Inference Acceleration of LLMs (2025)).
- For background, "Decoding Speculative Decoding" (arXiv:2402.01528) found that the performance of speculative decoding depends heavily on the latency of the draft model.

I found the paper you're looking for.

**Beat the long tail: Distribution-Aware Speculative Decoding for RL Training** (arXiv: 2511.13841)

**Authors and publication:** The authors are Zelei Shao, Vikranth Srivatsa (equal contribution), Sanjana Srivastava, Qingyang Wu, Alpay Ariyak, Xiaoxia Wu, Ameen Patel, Jue Wang, Percy Liang, Tri Dao, Ce Zhang, Yiying Zhang, Ben Athiwaratkun, Chenfeng Xu and Junxiong Wang, from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Together AI, UC San Diego and Prime Intellect. Version 1 was posted on Mon, 17 Nov 2025. The paper now also appears in the MLSys 2026 proceedings.

**The problem:** RL post-training is slowed down most by the rollout phase. The authors point to the long-tail distribution of rollout lengths, where a small fraction of long generations dominates wall-clock time. They also see an opportunity: historical rollouts that reveal stable prompt-level patterns across training epochs. As decoding goes on, short sequences finish first and the effective batch size shrinks, leaving a few long stragglers to determine the step makespan.

**The method (DAS):** DAS speeds up RL rollouts without altering model outputs. It has two main parts:
1. **Suffix-tree drafter:** A drafter that doesn't need training, built from recent rollouts using an incrementally maintained suffix tree. Each problem shard gets its own suffix tree speculator, which is updated from the most recent rollouts. At decode time, the speculator proposes multi-token drafts drawn from high-frequency suffix matches, and the target model verifies them in parallel.
2. **Length-aware speculation policy:** This allocates more aggressive draft budgets to long trajectories that dominate makespan. Problems predicted to be long or hard get a bigger speculative budget, while easy problems get little or none. The policy is updated over a sliding window of recent trajectories, so it keeps up as the policy changes during training.

The authors use a nonparametric drafter because the model being trained (the target model) keeps changing during RL training, so a fixed pre-trained draft model would fall out of step with it.

**Results:** On math and code reasoning tasks, DAS cuts rollout time by up to 50% while keeping training curves identical. The method is built on VeRL, and the up-to-50% reduction is measured directly against that baseline.

**Related work:**
- **TLT ("Taming the Long-Tail", arXiv 2511.16665):** Takes a similar approach, speeding up reasoning RL training without loss by adding adaptive speculative decoding, but it trains a draft model instead of using a suffix tree.
- **RhymeRL ("History Rhymes"):** Concurrent work that also uses speculative decoding and trajectory similarity to speed up RL rollouts.
- **SuffixDecoding** (Oliaro et al., arXiv:2411.04975): Earlier suffix-tree speculative decoding work that DAS cites.

Links: arXiv abstract at arxiv.org/abs/2511.13841, plus PDF and HTML versions.

The paper you're looking for is **"Distributed Speculative Inference (DSI): Speculation Parallelism for Provably Faster Lossless Language Model Inference."** It was presented as a poster at ICLR 2025.

**Authors:** Nadav Timor, Jonathan Mamou, Daniel Korat, Moshe Berchansky, Oren Pereg, Moshe Wasserblat, Tomer Galanti, Michal Gordon-Kiwkowitz, and David Harel.

**The problem it solves:** Earlier work on speculative inference (SI) showed it can be faster than normal one-token-at-a-time inference, but only if the small "drafter" models are fast and accurate enough, which often isn't true in practice. The authors show that SI can actually be slower than normal inference when the drafters are too slow or inaccurate. They close this gap by proving that DSI is faster than both SI and normal inference with any drafters. That means DSI can also speed up models that SI can't help. Like other SI methods, DSI works on frozen language models with no training or changes to the architecture, and it keeps the target model's output distribution.

**Speculation parallelism (SP):** DSI introduces a new type of task parallelism, called speculation parallelism, that runs copies of the target model and the drafters so they overlap in time. The "SP degree" is the largest number of target servers (servers that run the target model) used at the same time. In SI, checking the current drafts blocks the next round of drafting. DSI runs those checks on extra threads to hide their latency. This creates a new basic tradeoff between computing resources and latency.

**Results:** In simulations, DSI was 1.29–1.92x faster than SI in single-node setups across several off-the-shelf models and tasks. The code is open source. The guarantees hold for both single- and multi-node setups, but the experiments only covered single nodes with up to eight GPUs and an SP degree of 7 or less. Because of budget limits, the authors simulated access to such a node instead of running on a physical eight-GPU machine.

**Links:**
- ICLR poster page: iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/29058
- arXiv: 2405.14105 (first posted May 23, 2024; latest version v5 from March 15, 2025)
- ICLR 2025 proceedings PDF: proceedings.iclr.cc

**Related work:** The MagicDec paper, also at ICLR 2025, cites SP and notes that it overlaps target verification with draft speculation to enhance speedup. A later paper, "Speculative Speculative Decoding," describes DSI as an approach that overlaps drafting and verification, verifying multiple sequences in parallel with distinct logical copies of the verifier model.

## Missing lossless speculative decoding papers, ranked by importance

I checked every arXiv ID and month, and every venue except SwiftSpec's, by web search in October 2026. A venue is listed only where I found evidence for it. "arXiv only" means I found no acceptance.

| # | Short name | Full title | arXiv id (first month) | Venue | Core idea | Limitation of an existing node it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ReDrafter | Recurrent Drafter for Fast Speculative Decoding in Large Language Models | 2403.09919 (Mar 2024) | arXiv only. It is in TensorRT-LLM and Apple MLX. | RNN drafter on target hidden states, beam search, dynamic tree attention, distillation | **Medusa**: its heads ignore dependencies between drafted tokens and it uses a static tree |
| 2 | HASS | Learning Harmonized Representations for Speculative Sampling | 2408.15766 (Aug 2024) | ICLR 2025 | Multi-step context alignment plus top-K ranking distillation when training the draft head | **EAGLE-2**: the draft trains on true target features but sees its own noisy features at inference |
| 3 | Heterogeneous-vocab SD (SLEM / TLI / SLRS) | Accelerating LLM Inference with Lossless Speculative Decoding Algorithms for Heterogeneous Vocabularies | 2502.05202 (Jan 2025) | ICML 2025 (oral, per your list) | String-level matching or vocabulary intersection let any off-the-shelf drafter stay lossless | **Speculative Decoding**: the drafter and target must share one vocabulary |
| 4 | DSI | Distributed Speculative Inference (DSI): Speculation Parallelism for Provably Faster Lossless Language Model Inference | 2405.14105 (May 2024) | ICLR 2025 | "Speculation parallelism": several target replicas verify drafts concurrently, so verification does not block | **Speculative Decoding**: verification blocks drafting, and a slow or poor drafter can be slower than plain decoding |
| 5 | SSD / Saguaro | Speculative Speculative Decoding | 2603.03251 (Mar 2026) | ICLR 2026 | Draft runs on separate hardware and pre-speculates for likely verification outcomes during verification | **PEARL / AMUSD**: drafting stays on the critical path after a rejection, and fallbacks fail at large batch sizes |
| 6 | DSpark | DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation | 2607.05147 (Jul 2026) | arXiv only. Used in DeepSeek-V4 serving and in vLLM Speculators. | DFlash backbone, a light sequential correction head, and a confidence-scheduled draft length | **DFlash**: parallel positions are independent and conflict, and fixed blocks waste verification capacity at high batch |
| 7 | P-EAGLE | P-EAGLE: Parallel-Drafting EAGLE with Scalable Training | 2602.01469 (Feb 2026) | arXiv only. In vLLM since v0.16. | EAGLE-3 head drafts all K tokens in one pass using a learnable mask token and hidden state | **EAGLE-3**: its autoregressive drafter needs K sequential forward passes |
| 8 | QuantSpec | QuantSpec: Self-Speculative Decoding with Hierarchical Quantized KV Cache | 2502.10424 (Feb 2025) | ICML 2025 | Self-draft uses 4-bit weights and the upper 4 bits of a shared hierarchical INT8 KV cache | **TriForce / MagicDec**: sparse-KV self-drafts have low acceptance and need extra memory |
| 9 | SparseSpec (called SpecGen on the MLSys page) | Accelerating Large-Scale Reasoning Model Inference with Sparse Self-Speculative Decoding | 2512.01278 (Dec 2025) | MLSys 2026 (oral) | Self-draft uses dynamic sparse attention (PillarAttn), picking tokens from verification attention scores; aimed at long chain-of-thought | **MagicDec**: its static sparse-KV draft fits long reasoning outputs poorly |
| 10 | Optimal multi-draft SD | Multi-Draft Speculative Sampling: Canonical Decomposition and Theoretical Limits (Khisti et al.). | 11 | HSD | Overcoming Joint Intractability with Lossless Hierarchical Speculative Decoding | 2601.05724 (Jan 2026) | ICLR 2026 | Hierarchical branch resampling gives provably lossless sequence-level verification; +12% on EAGLE-3 | **Block Verification**: works from partial information and does not combine with multi-draft or trees |
| 12 | SpecDiff | Speculative Diffusion Decoding: Accelerating Language Generation through Diffusion | 2408.05636 (Aug 2024) | NAACL 2025 | A discrete diffusion LM drafts a whole block in one or two denoising steps | **Speculative Decoding**: an autoregressive drafter's cost grows linearly with draft length. This is the ancestor of DFlash. |
| 13 | GRIFFIN | GRIFFIN: Effective Token Alignment for Faster Speculative Decoding | 2502.11018 (Feb 2025) | NeurIPS 2025 | Training masks the loss to aligned tokens, and the draft head corrects its features with input tokens | **EAGLE-2/3** (via HASS): the token sequences seen in training and decoding still differ |
| 14 | SwiftSpec | SwiftSpec: Ultra-Low Latency LLM Decoding by Scaling Asynchronous Speculative Decoding | 2506.11309 (Jun 2025) | ASPLOS 2026 according to one third-party paper list (LLMSys-PaperList); not confirmed | Draft and target on separate GPU pools, parallel tree generation, tree-aware KV sync, fused kernels | **PEARL / AMUSD**: assume co-located models; a small drafter gains little from tensor parallelism; KV caches fall out of sync |
| 15 | SpecExec | SpecExec: Massively Parallel Speculative Decoding for Interactive LLM Inference on Consumer Devices | 2406.02532 (Jun 2024) | NeurIPS 2024 | Deterministic search builds draft trees of thousands of tokens as a cache for offloaded targets | **SpecInfer / Sequoia**: their trees are too small for offloading, where one verification can check thousands of tokens |
